title: Move the Xray pop-out onto the owned root, and keep Story embedding working
description:
CONTEXT IS ON THE PARENT EPIC rf2-k97c. Read it first — it is the durable record (the
analysis lived in an untracked ai/findings/ tree and is gone). Line numbers drift; verify.

FOLLOW-ON, after child .3: the pop-out and the Story embedding.

POP-OUT. Xray already has one, and it is NOT isolation — mount.cljs:1520 records that
"Everything Xray runs for the popout lives in the OPENER's JS realm": popout! is called from
the opener, the adapter's render paints the popout's DOM from there, popout-state is an
opener-realm atom, and the popout document runs no Xray code of its own. The second
adapter/render call site (:1688) is the pop-out's. When .3 gives Xray its own root, the
pop-out path must move with it, and its opener-reload watchdog must still work.
Distinguish a separate DOM root, a separate window and a separately booted JS runtime. This
bead is the first two only. A genuinely separate runtime (with a transport) is future work
and is NOT in scope here.

STORY EMBEDDING. Story embeds Xray panels. Story is itself Reagent-authored (39 reagent.core
requires; renders via rdc/create-root at ui/shell.cljs:1225). Account for the existing
embedding and keep it working; identify which ideas from .3 transfer.
SOLVING STORY'S OWN VIEW-SUBSTRATE ARCHITECTURE IS EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE. Do not let this
bead grow into that. If Story needs the same treatment, file it separately with its own
justification.

`rf/configure!` (`core.cljc:2554`) is the one process-config write door. `spec/Conventions.md:1283-1293` promises its read twin "on every facade" (`describe-config` / `current-config`) and the facade ships neither. ```clojure

(rf/current-config)   ; → {:epoch-history {…} :trace-buffer {…} :elision {…}}

title: api(registry): RULING — `:flow` / `:app-schema` / `:machine` in the query grammar, + two fable-only slices
description:
_Filed 2026-09-05 12:37:46 AUSEST by the API-review wave-3 coordinator from registry-introspection.md (ref registry-introspection.4); parent epic rf2-kuky. Local-only dossiers: ai/findings/API-review/{fable,codex}/ (gitignored; may be deleted)._

## Decision needed

After @registry-introspection.2 (one query map, `:source :store` XOR `:frame f`) and @registry-introspection.3 (the ten registrar-kind aliases deleted), three facts remain reachable only through bespoke doors with their own frame-argument shapes. Mike rules whether the grammar reaches them. Fable's doc proposes the ceiling; codex explicitly declined it; fable's own cross-check says "delete the registrar-kind aliases and adopt `:source` first (a two-reviewer finding), then decide whether `:flow`, `:app-schema` and `:machine` join the grammar (this doc's alone, and it needs a ruling)".

## The facts and their doors (tip 6445d0611b; unchanged since the dossier's tip by diff)

- Flows: `re-frame.flows/flows-snapshot` (`implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc:49`; `@flows` = `{frame-id {flow-id flow-map}}`, ALL frames) and `flow-meta-at` (`:77`; `(get-in @flows [f id])`, trailing `opts-or-frame`). The registrar `:flow` kind is reserved-EMPTY (`registrar.cljc:98-146`); .2 makes a `:flow` query throw `registrar-kind-not-queryable` naming these doors. Consumers: tools code 1 + 1 (Xray `static/flows/panel.cljs`), tests ~135 lines / 24 files.
- App-db schemas: `re-frame.schemas/app-schemas` (`schemas/storage.cljc:690`; `{path (:schema meta)}` for a frame), `app-schema-at` (`:649`), `app-schema-meta-at` (`:666`; the `{id meta}` value), all with a trailing `opts-or-frame-id` that sniffs keyword-vs-map; `app-schemas-digest` (`digest.cljc:138`, a SHA — a computation, kept by both reviewers). Xray's schemas panel rebuilds the `{path meta}` map by hand from two of them (`static/schemas/panel.cljs:298-304`) — codex names this loop as the one worthwhile follow-on ("expose one frame-schema metadata collection from the existing side-table seam"). Consumers: tools code 1 / 0 / 2, tests ~105 lines / 12 files.
- Machines: an `:event` registration with `:rf/machine? true` carrying its spec under `:rf/machine`. After .3 the read is a `filter` / `(:rf/machine (handler-meta …))`. The pair-MCP wire already presents `machine` as a KIND in the same enum as `event` / `route` / `resource` (`descriptors_data.cljs:1709, 1775`), translated tool-side.
- Five frame-targeting shapes coexist on this lane today (fable §The problem): sole positional target; `{:frame f …}` map; trailing `opts-or-frame-id` with type sniffing (the schemas fns, `flow-meta-at`, and `machine-by-system-id` — `machines.cljc:197-232`, which needs a `frame-value?` test because a frame value is itself a map); no frame form; all-frames-at-once (`flows-snapshot`).

## Options

**A — codex floor + one shape (RECOMMENDED; Grok's third option in the fable doc).** Side tables stay their own doors, but take the SAME map shape as the query grammar: `(rf.flows/flows {:frame f})` → `{flow-id flow-map}` (and `(rf.flows/flow-meta {:frame f :id id})`), `(rf.schemas/app-schemas {:frame f})` → `{path meta}` in one read (Xray's loop goes), `(rf.schemas/app-schema-meta {:frame f :path p})`; the trailing `opts-or-frame-id` sniffing goes; a frameless read of a frame-scoped store throws (the loud answer `(registrations :flow)` never gave); `flows-snapshot`'s all-frames read becomes `(into {} (map (juxt identity #(rf.flows/flows {:frame %}))) (rf/frame-ids))` at the one caller, or stays if Mike wants the whole-registry snapshot as a verb. `machine-by-system-id`'s 2-arity drops the sniffing: opts map only. Machines stay a filter; pair-MCP keeps translating its friendly `machine` category. One documented home per fact; no universal registry.

**B — fable ceiling.** `:flow` and `:app-schema` become FRAME-SCOPED kinds of `registrations` / `handler-meta` (map form with `:frame` only; `:source :store` on them throws), read through the artefacts' existing late-bind seams (`:schemas/frame-schema-entries`, `storage.cljc:712`, returns exactly `{path meta}`; a new `:flows/frame-flows` hook); `:machine` becomes a read-side projection kind (`{:source :store :kind :machine}` = `:event` filtered by `:rf/machine?`, meta = the `:rf/machine` spec); `:frame` leaves `kinds`; the five side-table fns are deleted. Cost fable states honestly: `registrations` grows a kind-dispatch seam to two optional artefacts and "the frame-scoped map read is a store read, not an image resolution, so the docstring must say the map form means 'through frame f' in two senses". Codex's objection (§Follow-on): "flow snapshots and app-schema collections are different stores with meaningful frame behavior … one reliable public way to inspect each fact does not require one universal registry for every fact"; Grok's: a virtual `:machine` kind "will fight 005's 'a machine IS an event handler' commitment the first time someone tries to `clear` or image-resolve it".

**C — stop after .2 and .3.** Leave the five doors and their three frame-arg shapes as they are.

## Two smaller fable-only slices to rule in the same breath

**(b) `rf/resources` / `rf/mutations`** (`resources.cljc:150`, `:229`; facade re-exports on `re-frame.core` ~`core.cljc:1520`, `:1560`; manifest rows `:173`, `:137`, `:303`-adjacent). Each bundles a registry alias (`:resource-ids` / `:mutation-ids`) with a runtime-db path read (`:entries` / `:instances`) that Xray already takes by path (`panels/resources_helpers.cljc:20-32`) and that `resource-state` / `mutation-state` serve per key. Consumers: examples 0, tools 0, tests 5 + 6 lines / 2 files. Fable: delete both; codex: silent (its list of ten getters omits them; it keeps "runtime resource state" as a separate fact without naming the fn). Recommendation: delete — the registry half is `(keys (rf/registrations {:source :store :kind :resource}))`, the runtime half is `resource-state` / `mutation-state` (kept, live-state lane, `spec/016-Resources.md:708-716` written discriminator). Touches `spec/API.md:466-467` (hot), 016 `:477, :570`, `docs/api/re-frame.core.md`, `re-frame.resources.md`, `skills/re-frame2/references/cross-cutting/api-cheatsheet.md:96`, two test files, manifest.

**(c) the nine `*-algebra-view` fns** (`routing/tooling.cljc`, `resources/tooling.cljc`, `flows/tooling.cljc`, `machines/tooling.cljc`, `subs/tooling.cljc`; JVM facade alias blocks at `routing.cljc:122-123`, `resources.cljc:110-111`, `machines.cljc:249-250`, `core/src/re_frame/subs.cljc:2535-2536`). Exactly one consumer: `re-frame.derivation.graph` resolves them by late-bound symbol (`derivation/graph.cljc:4-13`); Xray reads the composed graph; tools code 0, tests 122 lines / 8 files. Fable: demote from the `tooling` tier to the unrowed contributor seam `Derivations.md` already calls "no public accessor", deleting the four JVM alias blocks. Codex: not examined. Recommendation: demote (a manifest re-tier + four `def` deletions + `docs/api` sections such as `re-frame.routing.md` `route-algebra-view`); low value either way — fold into (a)'s bead if A is ruled, else file nothing.

## Recommendation

A + (b) + (c). It is the floor both reviewers reached plus the one shape rule that removes the type-sniffing trailing arg, and it keeps `registrations` meaning one storage model.

## Implementation beads to file when ruled

- A: ONE bead — `api(registry): side-table reads take the `{:frame f …}` map; delete trailing opts-or-frame sniffing` — files: `flows/registry.cljc:49-90`, `flows.cljc:40, 45` (facade defs), `schemas/storage.cljc:649-712`, `schemas.cljc:53-55`, `digest.cljc:138` (frame arg → map), `machines.cljc:197-232`; Xray `static/flows/panel.cljs`, `static/schemas/panel.cljs:292-306`, `panels/epoch/view.cljs` (2 sites per fable); tests ~240 lines / 36 files respelled; `spec/013-Flows.md:139`, `spec/010-Schemas.md:241`, `spec/API.md` §Schemas rows `:557-559` (hot), `spec/005-StateMachines.md` `machine-by-system-id` (hot), `docs/api/re-frame.{flows,schemas,machines}.md`, skills mentions (5 files for `app-schemas`), manifest regen. Plus (b) and (c) folded in or as one small sibling each.
- B: TWO beads, sequenced — (1) core dispatch seam + the two artefact hooks + error paths + `spec/001` §Registry model / `spec/API.md` / `002` (hot); (2) consumers, tests, `013` / `010` / `005` prose, docs, skills, manifest, deletion of the five fns. Both blocked by @registry-introspection.2 and @registry-introspection.3.
- C: nothing; close this bead with the reason.

## The problem

Every registrar kind is answered by one grammar: `(registrations kind)` → `{id meta}`, `(handler-meta kind id)` → `meta`, with `{:frame f …}` as the frame-targeted form. Beside it, each artefact grew a `<kind>-ids` / `<kind>-meta` pair. For the registrar kinds those pairs are one-line aliases (routing/registry.cljc:609-613 says so in its own comment: "The `<thing>-ids` + `<thing>-meta` enumerate pair every sibling registry carries"). For the three stores that are *not* registrar slots — flows, app-db schemas, frames — the pairs are the only door, because the generic query answers `{}` for `:flow` and `:frame` while both sit in the closed `kinds` set (registrar.cljc:144-145).

Five frame-targeting shapes coexist on this one lane: (a) a sole positional target (`frame-generation f`, `frame-meta id`, `sub-cache-snapshot f`); (b) a map with `:frame` plus coordinates (`registrations`, `handler-meta`, `resources`, `resource-state`, `mutation-state`); (c) a trailing `opts-or-frame-id` that sniffs keyword vs map (`app-schemas`, `app-schema-at`, `app-schema-meta-at`, `app-schemas-digest`, `flow-meta-at`), which `machine-by-system-id` has to extend with a `frame-value?` test because a frame value is itself a map (machines.cljc:224); (d) no frame form at all (every `*-ids` / `*-meta` alias, `machines`, `machine-meta`, `sub-topology`); (e) all frames at once (`flows-snapshot`).

Two facts show what the duplication costs. Xray's `machine_inspector.cljs:673-705` and `routing.cljs:477-487` say in their docstrings that they do NOT call `machines/machines`, `machine-meta` or `(rf/registrations :route)` but re-derive them over `host-registry/registrations`, because the positional generic form is ambiently generation-scoped inside a sub build (registrar.cljc:224-250 binds `*generation*`; `registrations` at :873 projects from it when bound) — while API.md §Public registrar query API promises the positional arity "reads the default source store … byte-identical". The tree contradicts the spec, and the workaround is a fourth spelling (`host-registry/registrations`, 18 lines / 9 files). Second: pair-MCP's `handler_meta.cljs:261` and `:386` emit eval forms naming `re-frame.core/machine-meta` and `re-frame.core/machines`, which `re-frame.core` no longer exports (moved to `re-frame.machines` by rf2-wad2fl; `rg` of core.cljc finds only docstring mentions). No live test reaches those strings (`handler_meta_test.cljs:657-700` exercises only the `:frame`-refusal branch), so `list-handlers {kind "machine"}` against a running app evaluates an undefined var. A per-kind name drifted; the generic query did not.

5. **Enumerate frame-scoped registrations** (flows, app-db schemas) for one frame — Xray flows/schemas panels, epoch view.
6. **Whole-registry snapshot across frames** — Xray static flows panel (`flows-snapshot`).
7. **Live-state reads** (resource entries, mutation instances, actor by system-id, sub cache) — a different lane; see Non-goals.

## Simpler elegant target

One grammar, two fns, one frame spelling:

```clojure
(registrations kind)                          ; {id meta} from the process store — never generation-scoped
(registrations kind pred)                     ; filtered
(registrations {:frame f :kind k :pred ?p})   ; {id meta} resolved through frame f (image kinds) or f's own store (frame-scoped kinds)
(handler-meta kind id)                        ; meta or nil
(handler-meta {:frame f :kind k :id id})
```

`kind` is the closed set `#{:event :sub :fx :cofx :interceptor :view :route :head :error-projector :resource :mutation :resource-scope :flow :app-schema :machine}`. `:flow` and `:app-schema` are **frame-scoped kinds**: the positional form throws the existing `:rf.error/registrar-query-needs-frame`, the map form reads the artefact's per-frame store through the late-bind seams that already exist (`:schemas/frame-schema-entries`, storage.cljc:712 — it returns exactly `{path meta}`; a `:flows/frame-flows` hook returning `(get @flows f)`). `:machine` is a **read-side projection** of `:event` filtered by `:rf/machine?` with meta = the `:rf/machine` spec — no new registrar slot, which keeps 005's architectural commitment; it is the kind pair-MCP already presents. `:frame` leaves the `kinds` roster: frames are not `reg-*` registrations, they are live runtime objects, and `frame-ids` / `frame-meta` stay as that lane's verbs. Positional `registrations` always reads the process store; `*generation*` is consulted only by the framework's own resolution paths, so a tool inside a sub build gets what API.md already promises and Xray's `host-registry` namespace is deleted.

Before / after, per use case:

```clojure
;; 1–2  enumerate + read a registrar kind
(rf.routing/route-ids)  (rf.routing/route-meta id)       ;; before
(keys (rf/registrations :route))  (rf/handler-meta :route id)   ;; after (already what tools do)


(rf/resource-meta id)                                   ;; before
(:rf/resource (rf/handler-meta :resource id))           ;; after

;; 4  machines
(rf.machines/machines)  (rf.machines/machine-meta id)   ;; before
(keys (rf/registrations :machine))  (rf/handler-meta :machine id)   ;; after — one string in pair-MCP's list-form goes away

;; 5  frame-scoped kinds
(rf.flows/flow-meta-at id {:frame f})                   ;; before (or `(flow-meta-at id f)` — same fn, keyword sugar)
(rf/handler-meta {:frame f :kind :flow :id id})         ;; after

(keys (rf.schemas/app-schemas f)) + (app-schema-meta-at path f) per path   ;; before — Xray's by-hand loop
(rf/registrations {:frame f :kind :app-schema})         ;; after — the {path meta} map in one read
(:schema (rf/handler-meta {:frame f :kind :app-schema :id path}))          ;; replaces app-schema-at

;; 6  all frames (Xray static flows panel)
(rf.flows/flows-snapshot)                               ;; before
(into {} (map (juxt identity #(rf/registrations {:frame % :kind :flow}))) (rf/frame-ids))   ;; after

;; 3  frame-resolved image read — unchanged
(rf/registrations {:frame f :kind :event})
```

**Deleted (15):** `route-ids`, `route-meta`, `resource-ids`, `mutation-ids`, `scope-resolver-ids`, `scope-resolver-meta`, `machines`, `machine-meta`, `flows-snapshot`, `flow-meta-at`, `app-schemas`, `app-schema-at`, `app-schema-meta-at`, `resources`, `mutations` (the last two bundle a registry alias with a runtime-db path read that Xray already takes by path — resources_helpers.cljc:26). `resource-meta` / `mutation-meta` become artefact-private (their 38 callers are all inside the resources artefact) and leave both facades.

**Kept:** `registrations`, `handler-meta`, `frame-generation`, `generation-diff`, `frame-ids`, `frame-meta`, `app-schemas-digest` (a real computation; its frame arg becomes `{:frame f}` only), `sub-topology` (a derived graph, not a registry read), and the live-state lane — `sub-cache-snapshot`, `resource-state`, `mutation-state`, `machine-by-system-id` (the `frame-or-opts` arity drops the keyword/frame-value sniffing: opts map only).

**Demoted:** the nine `*-algebra-view` fns have exactly one consumer, `re-frame.derivation.graph` resolving them by late-bound symbol (graph.cljc:541-547); Xray reads the composed graph (derivation_graph.cljs:382). They leave the `tooling` tier and the four JVM facade alias blocks (routing.cljc:122, resources.cljc:110, machines.cljc:249, subs.cljc:2535) and become the unrowed contributor seam Derivations.md:728/765/827 already calls "no public accessor".

## Why this is better (ethos)

- **Regularity over cleverness** (Principles.md:18) and Conventions' *One obvious way* (:1554): the question "what is registered?" has one answer shape, `{id meta}`, and one frame spelling. Fifteen names that each encode a kind in their identifier are the "multiple equivalent encodings" the principle names as a tax on tooling and generated code — and the tax was paid: pair-MCP pinned a facade name that then moved.
- **Public query surfaces** (Principles.md:52-56) names `registrations`, `handler-meta`, `frame-ids`, `frame-meta`, `sub-topology` as *the* contract. The per-kind pairs are not in that sentence; they are back-room doors onto the same tables.
- **No silent swallow** (Principles.md:83): `(registrations :flow)` returning `{}` while flows exist is a recognised input answered with silence, and it bit a real consumer (flows/panel.cljs:29). A frame-scoped kind that throws `registrar-query-needs-frame` on the positional form is the loud answer the error catalogue already has.
- **Name over place** (Principles.md:32): `{:frame f :kind k :id id}` is name-over-place; `opts-or-frame-id` trailing args are place plus type-sniffing, and `machine-by-system-id`'s `frame-value?` guard is the brittleness the principle predicts.
- **Low hidden context** (Principles.md:89): the positional read silently changing universe under a bound `*generation*` is exactly "behaviour not determined by visible inputs"; the `{:frame f}` map exists so the frame is visible, so the positional form should carry none.
- **Data before magic** and Clojure's "100 functions on one data structure": `{id meta}` composes with `keys`, `filter`, `select-keys`, `get` — `route-ids` is `keys`, `machines` is `filter`, Xray's schema loop is `registrations`. Simple vs easy: `route-ids` is *easy* (a name to recall) but complects the kind into the fn name; kind-as-data is *simple*, and it is what the MCP wire already speaks.
- **The front-porch / back-room split** (API.md §Tier taxonomy): all of this is `tooling`; shrinking the back room costs no app author anything — examples carry zero calls.

What it costs, honestly: `registrations` grows a kind-dispatch seam to two optional artefacts (late-bind, as `reg-flow` / `reg-app-schema` already do from `re-frame.core`); the frame-scoped map read is a *store* read, not an image resolution, so the docstring must say the map form means "through frame f" in two senses; `resource-meta` callers write one extra key-hop; ~170 test lines that pin `flows-snapshot` / `app-schema-at` / `machine-meta` move; and 005 §Querying machines is rewritten from "lens fns" to "read-side kind". The `:rf/resource` / `:rf/machine` slot projection could instead be flattened into the meta, but that is a registration-metadata change outside this area.

# Registration inspection: one query grammar over explicit sources

Review date: 2026-09-05. Status: proposal only. Tracking bead: `rf2-snkw`.

## Finding

The implementation exposes generic registration reads and a growing set of feature-specific “list IDs / get metadata” pairs. These mostly project facts already present in the registrar. Their names do not reliably tell the caller which registration source will be inspected.

[Core](../../../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc), at `registrations` and `handler-meta`, supports positional queries and frame-targeted map queries. The map form currently requires `:frame`; it is not a general query map. `registrations` additionally accepts a predicate either positionally or as `:pred` in the frame map.

Meanwhile, these feature queries repeat the enumerate/lookup operation:

| Current names | What their implementations read |
| --- | --- |
| `route-ids`, `route-meta` | [Routing registry](../../../../implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/registry.cljc): IDs and full metadata under `:route`. |
| `resource-ids`, `resource-meta` | [Resource registry](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/registry.cljc): IDs under `:resource`; the metadata getter extracts `:rf/resource`. |
| `mutation-ids`, `mutation-meta` | [Mutation registry](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/mutation_registry.cljc): IDs under `:mutation`; extracts `:rf/mutation`. |
| `scope-resolver-ids`, `scope-resolver-meta` | [Scope registry](../../../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/scope_registry.cljc): IDs under `:resource-scope`; extracts `:rf/resource-scope`. |
| `machines`, `machine-meta` | [Machines](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines.cljc): filter `:event` registrations by `:rf/machine?`, then read their `:rf/machine` specs. Machines are not a separate registrar kind. |

These are not all byte-identical aliases: some return an inner specification rather than the outer registration metadata. That distinction should be documented as a data projection, not obscured by calling every result “meta.”

## Known use cases and empirical evidence

| Use case | Evidence | Requirement to retain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enumerate host definitions while an inspector runs in its own frame | [Xray host registry](../../../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/host_registry.cljs) | A reliable source-store read independent of the inspector's bound generation. |
| Inspect exactly the definitions selected by a live frame | Core's frame-targeted reads; [Story frame composition](../../../../tools/story/src/re_frame/story/frames.cljc), particularly variant image composition/allocation | Inspect a sealed frame generation, not a merge with whichever definitions happen to be globally registered now. |
| Get source coordinates for navigation and inspection | [Pair handler metadata](../../../../tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/handler_meta.cljs) | Singular lookup, full outer metadata, namespace/image provenance and source information. |
| List machine definitions and get their specs | [Xray machine inspector](../../../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/machine_inspector.cljs), `machine-definitions-value`; Pair's machine query forms | Preserve the distinction between a registered machine definition and a live machine instance. |
| Inspect resource and scope-resolver specifications | [Xray resources helpers](../../../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/resources_helpers.cljc) | Access both full metadata and the inner `:rf/resource` / `:rf/resource-scope` values. |
| Filter a catalogue or enumerate IDs | The generic predicate arities and feature list helpers | Ordinary map filtering and key projection; no additional query language is necessary. |
| Find a guard/action's definition | Core's `handler-meta :machine-guard` / `:machine-action` handling | Derived source metadata for composite IDs; these are not standalone registrar rows. |
| Inspect materialized flows and frame-local schema collections | [Xray flows panel](../../../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/static/flows/panel.cljs), [schemas panel](../../../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/static/schemas/panel.cljs) | These are different state stores/views; generic registration reads must not pretend to replace them. |

The reviewed example applications primarily register and use their own known IDs; I found no direct example-app demand for the feature getter families in the qualified-call searches. Tooling is the concrete consumer driving this finding. That is substantial demand in an AI-first library, not a reason to discard inspection.

## The source ambiguity is already costing a real tool

Core's positional docstrings describe the default process-global source store. However, [registrar](../../../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/registrar.cljc) lookup/enumeration honor a bound `*generation*`. Xray's subscriptions run under Xray's own image generation, so its host-registry adapter directly dereferences `kind->id->metadata` to see the host definitions instead of its own.

This is not evidence that frame isolation should be weakened. It is evidence that a public inspection request should explicitly identify the source it means. More `resource-meta`-style helpers would not solve that problem.

## Proposed smaller API

Keep two operations: enumerate a kind, or look up one definition. Give both the same map grammar with exactly one source selector: `:source :store`, or `:frame f`.

```clojure
;; PROPOSED source-store forms; these maps are rejected today.
(rf/registrations {:source :store :kind :route})
(rf/handler-meta {:source :store :kind :route :id :app/home})

;; Existing frame concept, shared grammar.
(rf/registrations {:frame app-frame :kind :event})
(:rf/resource
  (rf/handler-meta {:frame app-frame :kind :resource :id :articles/list}))

;; Ordinary Clojure projections, not more library operations.
(keys (rf/registrations {:source :store :kind :resource}))
(into {}
      (filter (fn [[_ metadata]] (:rf/machine? metadata)))
      (rf/registrations {:frame app-frame :kind :event}))
```

Under this proposal, `:source :store` explicitly bypasses inherited generation bindings. `:frame` keeps the existing precise frame resolution and failure behavior. Supplying both, or neither, is an invalid query, not an invitation to choose an ambient default. Retire positional reads, the generic predicate overloads, and the ten feature-specific public getters above. Preserve efficient singular lookup: a tool should not fetch an entire catalogue just to navigate to one definition.

Machine guard/action source queries can retain their existing derived meaning under the same source-store map grammar; they need not become new registries. Frame-targeted machine definition inspection uses the actual `:event` metadata. Extending frame-targeted derived guard/action inspection is not required to make this reduction useful.

Inner metadata keys become an explicitly supported projection contract. Full descriptors, source coordinates and provenance remain available. Feature internals may keep private helpers, and tools may retain user-friendly commands such as “list machines”; the reduction is in the library vocabulary, not the quality of its tools.

## Counterargument and migration

A named `resource-meta` helper is discoverable and hides the storage layout. Removing it makes a one-off call longer and commits the public model to the documented descriptor projection. That tradeoff is acceptable only if the generic API is genuinely usable: explicit sources, reliable data, concise examples, and stable metadata keys. “Use the private atom” is not the proposed API.

Migrate Xray's source bypass first, then frame-specific inspector queries and Pair's query generation. Preserve ID-set meaning without promising the old helpers' incidental vector order; use `(vec (keys ...))` only where a consumer actually requires a vector. Review every positional call for its intended source rather than globally rewriting it to the store: some currently rely on inherited frame resolution.

Keep frame metadata, live machine lookup, flow snapshots, app-schema collections/digests and runtime resource state separate. Those represent other facts, not alternative getters for the same row.

## Why this is more elegant

The domain has definitions, kinds, IDs, and resolution sources. It does not need a new pair of operations every time a feature defines a new kind. Clojure already supplies selection, filtering and projection over maps.

This follows the project's [public query surfaces and regularity principles](../../../../spec/Principles.md): a programmer or AI learns two operations and a data model, while an inspector can state precisely whose definitions it is observing. Fewer names are valuable here because they eliminate source ambiguity and repeated tool adapters, not merely because an API manifest gets shorter.

## Focused acceptance evidence

Exercise source-store reads from inside an image-isolated Xray subscription; compare two live frames with different selections/replacements; verify singular metadata and source navigation, machine filtering, missing IDs and invalid sources. Migrate the cited resource/machine panels and Pair queries without direct registrar-atom access. Do not redesign image composition or the registrar's storage while doing this.

## Follow-on comparison with Fable

[Fable's registry review](../fable/registry-introspection.md) independently reinforces removing per-kind projections and points to Pair's stale machine-query spellings. Its larger proposal also pulls frame-local flows/app-schemas and virtual machine kinds into the generic query grammar. I would retain the narrower boundary here: machines already have event descriptors, while flow snapshots and app-schema collections are different stores with meaningful frame behavior. The valuable common rule is one reliable public way to inspect each fact, not necessarily one universal registry for every fact.

The second reread found that Fable's later cross-check now adopts this document's explicit store/frame map grammar and keeps composite guard/action lookup derived. Those are converged recommendations; the broader side-table unification remains a separate proposal, not a prerequisite.

## Codex Recommendation

Choose **A — separate side-table reads with a common frame-map spelling — retaining `flows-snapshot`; yes to (b), yes to (c) as API demotion only**. This is worthwhile pre-alpha simplification, but the dossier overstates the equivalence of some deletions and understates actual consumers. The desired result is easier, reliable inspection, not the smallest possible function count.

The main diagnosis holds. [Core's query implementation](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc) enters a frame's generation resolution, whereas [flows](../../implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc) and [schemas](../../implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/storage.cljc) read their own frame-keyed stores. The schema collection already contains full metadata internally; [Xray's schema panel](../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/static/schemas/panel.cljs) needlessly reconstructs it through enumeration and repeated singular reads. One metadata collection read removes that loop and, by reading one immutable map, avoids mixing metadata from separate reads during concurrent registration. That latter benefit is an inference from the code, not a reproduced race. Qualified-call searches found no direct example/testbed callers, but these tools are substantial first-class consumers under [Public query surfaces](../../spec/Principles.md#public-query-surfaces).

Adopt A's `flows` / `flow-meta` and `app-schemas` / `app-schema-meta` map forms. Return full schema metadata in the collection and use `:schema` for the value projection. Keep direct singular lookup, including its existing path normalization. Document the chosen explicit-frame grammar once; retain documented ambient convenience only where the operation intentionally supports it, such as `machine-by-system-id`. Do not accidentally make an absent explicit target fall back to a global default. Internal hooks need not inherit every public arity change: `frame-schema-entries` remains a valid implementation seam. Also, deleting schema `coerce-opts` is not automatically part of a read cleanup: `reg-app-schemas` and registration error enrichment still use it in [storage.cljc](../../implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/storage.cljc). Preserve those write contracts within this change.

**Keep `flows-snapshot`.** It is a coherent whole-store operation with named demand, not simply another spelling of a one-frame lookup. [Flow algebra tooling](../../implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/tooling.cljc) uses it at both arities, including its all-frame static projection, in addition to Xray's flows panel. The proposed `frame-ids` plus repeated per-frame reads consults two different registries and changes one atom dereference into several reads. [Frame enumeration](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/frame.cljc) also applies lifecycle/visibility filtering. The composition therefore does not establish snapshot equivalence; on the JVM, intervening mutations can additionally produce a mixed-time result. Retaining the existing tiny accessor preserves useful power and avoids an unnecessary broad respelling.

The strongest argument for B is discoverability: an agent learns one request shape and asks for any category without learning artefact namespaces. A read facade can legitimately abstract different stores, and a virtual machine projection does not inherently violate the fact that machines are events. Those are viable designs, not architectural impossibilities. Nevertheless, B makes `:frame` select a sealed definition image for some kinds and mutable owned state for others, adds optional-artefact dispatch, and still cannot replace digest or live-state operations. A gives the current consumers the useful regularity with fewer semantic exceptions. B′ offers even less: [Pair already translates machine requests](../../tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/handler_meta.cljs), so keep the filtered event descriptors. C is a defensible deferral after .30/.31 fix the actual registrar problems; I prefer A because this is the inexpensive stage to settle the public grammar.

For **(b), yes**, remove the mixed `resources` / `mutations` summaries. [Their bodies](../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources.cljc) bundle registration IDs with unrelated runtime collections; [Xray already reads the documented reserved runtime paths](../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/resources_helpers.cljc). However, `resource-state` / `mutation-state` alone are not replacements for enumeration. The migration must explicitly show the whole-table runtime-db read alongside the registry query. Preserve resource byte-string keys and mutation instance IDs; projecting resource entries onto their human-readable scoped vectors can collapse distinct entries. Keep the existing runtime assertions while changing only their access recipe.

For **(c), yes to reducing the supported API tier**, but correct the consumer inventory. [Xray's `xray-contributors`](../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/derivation_graph.cljs) directly references all nine functions as values under `:static-fn` / `:live-fn`. A census of invocation forms misses these real users. The [graph composer](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/derivation/graph.cljc) resolves optional contributors on the JVM and accepts supplied contributors on CLJS. Preserve callable implementation vars and that wiring; remove convenience aliases and update generated API classification. This matches [Derivations' internal-contributor design](../../spec/Derivations.md), without deleting supported graph behavior or its explanatory documentation.

Implement after .30/.31, updating the owned schemas/flows APIs, consumers, manifest and teaching material together. Acceptance should center on existing [divergent-frame flow tests](../../tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/static/flows/panel_cljs_test.cljs) and [schema metadata/isolation tests](../../implementation/schemas/test/re_frame/schemas_storage_test.clj), plus the Pair schema response, Xray graph assembly, and unchanged digest bytes. title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: implementation/core frames, images and registration
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: implementation/core frames, images and registration. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.9 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.9 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.9 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.9) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/core frames, images and registration. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/core frames, images and registration. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/core frames, images and registration to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/core frames, images and registration; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/core frames, images and registration plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/core frames, images and registration that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: routing: with-base-path with base "/" may emit a protocol-relative //path href (suspected, unreproduced)
description:
Found by the rf2-nvxtm.23 worker (routing pruning, PR #11202) by reading the code, NOT reproduced. Re-derive at tip.

implementation/routing strategy.cljc: `with-base-path` with a base of "/" appears to produce a protocol-relative href such as `//active` for route `/active`. A browser resolves `//active` as a different HOST ("active"), so links under a root base path would navigate off-site.

TASK: reproduce first with a JVM test (`with-base-path` "/" applied to a path like "/active" must yield "/active"). Check the neighbouring cases too: base "" , base "/app", base "/app/", and a path without a leading slash. If it reproduces, fix the join so it never emits a leading "//", and keep the test as the regression guard (red before, green after). If it does not reproduce, record the evidence and close. Exact fix only.
Gates: the routing JVM lane (clojure -M:test from implementation/routing) and the routing prod gate (scripts/test-routing-prod-gate.sh), counts before and after; clj-kondo on touched source, run without --fail-level. If the fix sits in a #?(:cljs) branch, say so and rely on CI's :node-test.

Worker dispatched in worktree C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2-worktrees/fix-routing-base-path, branch worker/fix-routing-base-path, off origin/main 6c517b054d. Packet fix-routing-base-path-fe4222ff2f35. Reproduce first; fix only if it reproduces.
== WORKER RESULT (2026-10-14 18:27:25 AUSEST): REPRODUCED and FIXED, PR #11211 (draft until handoff)
Cause: normalize-base-path in implementation/routing strategy.cljc stripped a trailing slash only when the base was longer than one character, so base "/" stayed "/" and with-base-path's :encode joined it onto the path-form href: (str "/" "/active") = "//active", a protocol-relative reference to host "active". So nil, blank and all-slash bases normalize to "" and with-base-path returns the strategy unchanged: the root is no base.   caller passes and the contract does not mention.

- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/security and implementation/test-quiet that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Pair tool describe-image rethrows for a frame made without :images; Xray README and skill still say the Frames tab lists only :images frames
description:
Follow-up to rf2-bmrh9 (PR #11235) and rf2-0fw90 (PR #11239), found by rf2-0fw90's worker. Since rf2-bmrh9, a frame made without `:images` (most apps' main frame) carries no sealed generation; it resolves the registration store live.

1. BUG, the pair tool: `describe-image` in skills/re-frame2-pair/preload/re_frame2_pair/runtime.cljs treats a frame as having no generation only when its id appears in the thrown error's `:live-frame-ids`, and that list holds only frames made WITH `:images`. For a live-store frame, `(rf/frame-generation :app/live)` throws with `{:live-frame-ids []}`, so `describe-image` RETHROWS. The AI pair cannot describe the main frame of most apps. Make it report such a frame as resolving the live store (the shape rf2-bmrh9's notes intended: `:no-generation? true`, or a clearer `:live-store? true`, and say which), with its registrations through the public `(rf/registrations {:frame f :kind k})` and its ambiguous ids named, as Xray's Frames tab now does (#11239, `image_view_reads/live-store-frames`). Reproduce first: a test that describes a frame made with `rf/make-frame` and no `:images` fails at base and passes after.
2. TEXT: tools/xray/README.md's Frames row, and the skills/re-frame2-xray pages that describe the Frames tab, still say it lists only frames made with `:images`. Since #11239 it lists live-store frames too, marked "live registration store", with ambiguous ids first.

Gates: the pair tool's own test lane (find it, and say which), the skills drift checks for touched skills files (scripts/check_skill_*.py, self-test and live), and scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci for the README.

title: The plain-atom and SSR adapters keep every frame's sub-cache across destroy-adapter!; call the existing clear-all-frame-sub-caches! helper
description:
The plain-atom and SSR adapters keep every frame's sub-cache across `destroy-adapter!`.

## The contract

Spec 006 says the adapter's `dispose-adapter!` "disposes every frame's sub-cache as part of process teardown". See §Lifetime contract → Adapter symmetry, and the contract table's "release listeners, caches, host resources". `rf/destroy-adapter!` leaves frames alive, so each adapter has to clear their caches itself.

## The defect

Two adapters do not:
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/plain_atom.cljc` (~L145): `(defn- dispose-adapter! [] ;; Watch handles are GC'd with their atoms; nothing else to clean up. nil)`
- `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/substrate.cljc` (~L57): `ssr-dispose-adapter!` has the same no-op body.

The helper for this already exists. `re-frame.subs.cache/clear-all-frame-sub-caches!` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/subs/cache.cljc` ~L514) is documented as having been lifted into CLJC so that CLJC adapters can satisfy Spec 006 §Adapter disposal lifecycle MUST 1. Only `implementation/adapters/test-react/src/re_frame/adapter/test_react.cljc` (~L431) calls it, and `test_react_dispose_sub_cache_cljs_test.cljc` pins that call.

## Change

Call the helper from both no-op disposers, as test-react does. Leave the hiccup emitter alone and the spines unchanged.

Do NOT move the walk into core's `dispose-adapter!`. Routed disposal hooks close when the generation is claimed, so that move belongs to the larger "adapter capabilities on the adapter map" refactor.

## Gates and provenance

No hot-zone file. Gates: the JVM core and SSR lanes, plus `npm run test:cljs` for the CLJS plain-atom path (that needs a lane grant).

Found by Sol 05 §4, and carried in Opus core-reactive-substrate §9 and action 4. Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\sol-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\05-core-subscriptions-substrates.md` §4.

2. The existing test-react and spine dispose tests stay green.

title: Delete the machines' process-side spawn-order cache (its docstring calls it WRONG about liveness); actor-live? reads the live runtime-db
description:
Delete the machines' process-side spawn-order cache. `actor-live?` can read the frame's live runtime-db directly, as it already does once the cache says yes.

## Where

`implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/spawn_order.cljc` keeps a transient `spawn-order` atom beside the durable `[:rf.runtime/machines :spawn-order]` vector.

Its own docstring (~L47) says it is "not merely stale, it is WRONG about liveness" after a restore, and gives it exactly one job: telling `destroy/actor-live?` that a drain-time `old-db` is stale. That clause is `(and (some #(= actor-id %) (frame-order frame-id)) (snapshot-present? (rf.frame/frame-runtime-db-value frame-id) actor-id))`. It only gates a live read that is itself a cheap `get-in`.

## Change

Make the third clause of `actor-live?` an unconditional live read. Then delete:
- `record!`, `forget!`, `frame-order`, `clear-frame!`, `reset-all!` and the atom;
- their call sites in `spawn.cljc` (~L1289), `destroy.cljc` (~L303), `finalize.cljc` (~L741), `frame_destroy.cljc` (~L292) and `machines.cljc` (~L464);
- the `:machines/reset-spawn-order!` hook, in core's `late_bind/directory.cljc` and in `test_support.cljc`.

This also removes the "finished actor stays recorded" hazard that `finalize.cljc` comments on.

Keep:
- the durable vector;
- the reverse-creation walk;
- every exact-incarnation fence.

## Spec text

Spec 005 §Destroy is silent-idempotent (~L2932-2939) calls the spawn-order entry "the reliable 'alive' bit", which already misdescribes the code. Rewrite it to say an actor is alive when its snapshot is present in the drain's runtime-db or in the frame's live runtime-db. Also update `spec/Runtime-Subsystems.md` (~L296, "spawn-order helpers"). rf2-7du80 edits other sections of that file.

Both reviews reached this step independently, separately from the larger entry-stamp work.

## Sequencing

**`spec/005-StateMachines.md` is a HOT ZONE**: this depends on rf2-iv1mw, which comes after rf2-yu0kh.

Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\opus-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\machines.md` §5 and action 3, and `...\sol-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\11-machines.md` §6.

1. A spawn and a destroy back to back in one `:fx` vector still tear the actor down.
2. A destroy after a restore that rewinds past a spawn is a silent no-op.
3. The incarnation-fence suites stay green, with their `frame-order` assertions moved to the durable order or dropped.
4. `spawn-order/record!` and `:machines/reset-spawn-order!` have no hits. The machines JVM and CLJS lanes are green.

title: Unit-test pruning: pair-mcp
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Unit-test pruning: bench-fresco
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to bench/fresco. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under bench/fresco. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside bench/fresco. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
bench/fresco to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in bench/fresco; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If bench/fresco plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside bench/fresco that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.
